CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in the back of the right heel, radiating up into the calf, after workouts and on first waking in the morning.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient Dennis presents with right posterior heel pain that is worse after workouts and on first rising in the morning. He describes the pain as extending up into the calf. He reports that on waking, the heel feels very tight, almost like it is tearing, and eases somewhat after about 10 to 15 minutes of walking. He reports the pain returns if he sits for an extended period and then tries to stand, and also gets sore after a lot of activity. He is training for a triathlon. He runs about 10 kilometers in the morning, bikes about 45 minutes to 1 hour at lunchtime, and swims about 30 minutes to 1 hour in the evening. He trains five days a week, alternating long runs and long bike sessions, with swimming on the other days, and takes one day off. He does not stretch, stating he does not have time. He reports he goes slowly at the start of runs until warmed up. The pain is mainly on the right side.

The doctor stated that the presentation could be plantar fasciitis; this was the doctor's initial impression and was not confirmed in the final assessment.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Lower extremity examination performed. Pain with passive dorsiflexion (pulling toes toward the body) on the right, described by the patient as "a little bit." Pain with resisted plantarflexion (pushing against the examiner) on the right, described as "a little bit." Left calf squeeze painless; right calf squeeze painless. Thompson test negative. Significant pain with squeezing of the right heel. Tenderness along the right Achilles tendon with palpation proximally up the tendon ("real tender").

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Achilles tendinitis of the right leg, per the doctor, attributed to overuse in the setting of aggressive triathlon training.

Plan:
- Stop training for one to two weeks, per the doctor.
- Ibuprofen (Advil), three tablets every six hours, as an anti-inflammatory, per the doctor.
- Referral for a couple of physical therapy visits for strengthening and stretching instruction.
- Return visit seven to ten days after the first physical therapy appointment to monitor progress.
- No x-ray indicated at this time, per the doctor.
- If pain persists at ten days with significant pain and no change despite activity modification, the doctor stated more aggressive treatment may be needed.
- Patient agreed with the plan ("sounds good").

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up of chronic problems: depression, hypertension, and status post rotator cuff repair.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Edward is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, hypertension, and prior rotator cuff repair who presents for followup of chronic problems. The doctor has not seen him in a while.

Depression: The patient reports doing pretty well over the past six months. At the last visit he was trying to develop new strategies to manage his depression and did not want to start medication because he is already on several medications. He sees a counselor once a week and has been swimming at the pool frequently over the summer and fall. He reports his depression is going well. He does not feel a need to start medication at this time and knows he can call if he does.

Hypertension: The patient reports good days and bad days. He takes his medication daily. He notes that occasional burgers and wine, as well as salt intake, sneak into his diet. He takes Norvasc. He checks his blood pressure at a CVS pharmacy kiosk about once a week.

Rotator cuff repair: Performed about eight months ago. The patient reports it is doing well. He has been stretching with a yoga ball and getting stronger, and he can continue this once a week. He has progressed from supervised physical therapy at the center to exercises at home.

Edema: The patient reports mild ankle swelling, mainly near the end of the day, which resolves by the next morning. The doctor stated this might be due to poor circulation, though the doctor was not sure. The doctor also suggested that it may be related to salt intake.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient completed a review of systems sheet at check-in. Patient denies nasal congestion, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Positive for intermittent ankle swelling as described in the HPI.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure: 156/94 mmHg in clinic.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, which the doctor notes has been heard previously and seems stable.
Lungs: Clear.
Lower extremities: 1 to 2+ pitting edema bilaterally in the legs.
Other systems: Doctor reports everything else on physical exam looks good.

RESULTS
Labs: Creatinine stable; the doctor reports that the lab results overall look good.
EKG: Normal per the doctor, with no evidence of coronary artery disease.
Home/pharmacy blood pressure readings: The doctor reviewed readings and notes they have been running a little high over the past couple of months.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Depression: Doing well per the doctor's assessment, with good coping strategies and a good support system. The doctor agrees that medication is not needed at this time. Patient may call if he wishes to start medication.

2. Hypertension: The doctor does not believe it is well controlled at this time. Plan to increase Norvasc to 10 mg daily. Order echocardiogram and lipid panel. Dietary counseling on decreasing salt intake was discussed.

3. Lower extremity edema: Bilateral 1 to 2+ pitting edema on exam. The doctor suggested it may be related to salt intake and possibly poor circulation, though this was stated as uncertain. Plan to discuss diet and decreasing salt intake.

4. Status post rotator cuff repair: Doing well. The doctor recommends continuing home exercises. No further intervention is needed, as the problem appears essentially resolved.

Patient has no questions.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for blood sugar control, blood pressure, cholesterol, leg and foot symptoms, and tobacco use.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a female, date of birth 03/05/1946, who consented to the visit being recorded. She reports feeling "same, pretty good." She received the doctor's letter about her prior results, which showed sugars not well controlled with A1c 9.9. Per the doctor, the plan at the prior visit was to increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day. At this visit, the patient reports she is still taking 2 mg. She has just filled her glimepiride prescription.

Diet: Patient reports she has not had pasta and does not keep it in the house. She rarely has bread; when she does, she buys wheat bread, usually two slices in the morning. She occasionally has peanut butter sandwiches. She drinks little soda and drinks club soda or seltzer water rather than plain water.

Eye care: Patient gets eye exams at a group practice on Liberty Road and reports her doctors there change at each visit. She saw Dr. Sanchez about a year ago and recently got a new prescription from him after cataract treatment. She reports a month of healing after the procedure. She is not happy with one lens; the other eye is good.

Blood pressure: Patient reports a home reading of 116 "on the dot" a couple of weeks ago. She reports taking her blood pressure medications.

Cholesterol and vascular disease: Patient is taking atorvastatin and reports tolerating it "okay." She reports constant foot discomfort, "my feet feel like hell," and leg pain that limits walking. She reports pain extending up to the hip. She states, "it might be sciatica, I'm not sure." She reports trying to walk more.

Tobacco: Patient reports she is still smoking and is not ready to quit. She says she will think about it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Patient denies fever and chills.
Neurologic: Patient denies headaches and dizziness. She reports feeling "totally normal" otherwise.
Eyes: Patient reports one lens is not satisfactory; the other is good.
Respiratory: Patient reports recent cough with congestion. Sputum is relatively clear. She denies shortness of breath. She reports the cough was better this morning.
Cardiovascular: Patient denies chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
Gastrointestinal: Patient denies nausea, vomiting, and other GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: Patient reports a slower urinary stream, which she attributes to age and states is stable. She urinates several times per day. She gets up at night occasionally, about once in a while. She notes she drinks fluids in the evening.
Musculoskeletal: Patient reports leg pain and hip pain extending into the upper legs, described as relatively stable per the doctor.
Extremities: Patient reports constant foot discomfort.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotid arteries normal. No bruits.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, normal rate. S1 and S2 crisp. No murmurs heard today.
Respiratory: Lungs clear. No rales or wheezing heard today.
Extremities: No edema. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable bilaterally.
Skin and nails: Thickened nails. Mildly dry skin. No skin breakdown.
Neurologic: Mildly decreased sensation in the tips of the first and second toes.

RESULTS
Prior A1c: 9.9 (per doctor, from the previous visit; the doctor stated the blood sugar average was above nine).
Blood pressure, clinic recheck today: 140/60 (per doctor). Patient's home reading a couple of weeks ago: 116 (per patient).
Labs: Blood work, including kidney function, to be drawn today. No results available at this visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Blood sugars not well controlled (A1c 9.9 at prior check).
- Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice a day. Patient to take two of her current 2 mg tablets twice a day until the new prescription is obtained.
- New prescription written for 4 mg tablets: one tablet twice a day once filled.
- Continue metformin.
- Counseled on hypoglycemia warning signs (weakness, shakiness, sweating) and to report them. Doctor does not expect this to occur.
- Labs to be rechecked today.
- Dietary counseling: reduce the number of wheat bread slices per day.

2. High blood pressure.
- Doctor reports clinic reading of 140/60 and states home numbers are better.
- Continue current combination: metoprolol 50 mg once daily, lisinopril with hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg once daily, and amlodipine 10 mg once daily. Patient reports taking all of these.
- Recheck blood pressure as planned.

3. High cholesterol and vascular disease in the legs.
- Continue high-dose atorvastatin (Lipitor) to protect the arteries.
- Patient reports leg and hip pain, described by the doctor as relatively stable. Patient is encouraged to continue walking. Patient suggests the leg pain might be sciatica; the doctor did not confirm this.

4. Peripheral neuropathy, feet (per doctor, "I think" this is what it is).
- Keep feet moisturized.
- Doctor notes a medication option if symptoms worsen, but the patient is already on many medications; no new medication started.
- Patient plans to purchase her own foot cream or scrub.

5. Cataracts, status post surgery.
- Vision improved per patient, though she is unhappy with one lens. Doctor noted laser cleanup may be possible, pending the eye doctor's assessment.
- Continue regular eye exams at the optometry group.

6. Cough with congestion.
- Patient reports clear sputum and that the cough improved this morning. Lungs clear on exam. No fever, chills, or shortness of breath reported.

7. Urinary symptoms.
- Patient reports slower stream, stable per doctor, with frequent urination and occasional nocturia. Patient attributes slow stream to age. Patient drinks fluids in the evening.

8. Tobacco use.
- Patient continues to smoke and is not ready to quit. Doctor advised her to quit; patient says she will think about it.

Other: No changes to other medications. Return visit in four months.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and peripheral vascular disease.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Maria Martin, date of birth 03/05/1946, consented to having this visit recorded. The patient reports her condition as "same I guess, pretty good." She received the doctor's letter about recent results, and the doctor stated her blood sugars are not well controlled. The patient is still taking glimepiride 2 mg. Per the prior letter, after an A1c of 9.9, glimepiride was to be increased to 4 mg twice daily. The patient has recently filled her prescription. Instructed to take two of the 2 mg tablets twice daily using current supply, with a new prescription for 4 mg tablets twice daily to follow. Patient was counseled to watch for hypoglycemia symptoms (weakness, shakiness, sweating) and report them.

Diet: The patient reports avoiding pasta, rarely keeping bread at home, and choosing wheat bread when she does have it. She usually eats two slices of bread in the morning and occasionally has peanut butter sandwiches. The doctor advised reducing the number of bread slices per day, including wheat bread. The patient reports she rarely drinks soda and drinks club soda or seltzer water, not plain water.

Eye care: The patient reports her eye exams are up to date and she recently received new glasses. She sees a provider at the Liberty Road group (Optimum Optometrists), with varying doctors each visit; she prefers Dr. Sanchez, whom she saw about a year ago and more recently for a prescription. She had cataract surgery, and after a one-month healing period, her prescription was written. She is not happy with one lens. The doctor mentioned that laser treatment might be possible, pending the eye specialist's assessment.

Hypertension: The patient reports a home blood pressure of 116 on a recent check. She reports taking metoprolol 50 mg once daily, lisinopril with hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg once daily, and amlodipine 10 mg once daily. The doctor's recheck in clinic was 140/60.

Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: The patient is taking atorvastatin and tolerates it, per her report. She reports persistent foot discomfort ("my feet feel like hell"), constant leg pain limiting walking, and pain extending up to the hips and upper legs. The doctor stated that the feet symptoms may represent peripheral neuropathy. The doctor also stated that the leg symptoms might be sciatica, though this was noted as uncertain. The doctor described the leg and hip symptoms as relatively stable. The patient reports she is trying to walk.

Tobacco: The patient continues to smoke and is not ready to quit. She states she will think about it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Patient denies fever and chills.
Neurologic: Patient denies headaches and dizziness. Reports foot and leg pain as above.
Respiratory: Patient reports recent cough with congestion, with relatively clear sputum. Denies shortness of breath. Per the patient, the cough improved this morning.
Cardiovascular: Patient denies chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
Gastrointestinal: Patient denies nausea, vomiting, and GI symptoms.
Genitourinary: Patient reports slower urinary stream, described as stable, and urination several times per day. Nocturia is occasional ("once in a while"). She attributes slower urination to age and notes she tends to drink fluids in the evening.
Ophthalmologic: Patient reports vision is improved after cataract surgery, with dissatisfaction with one lens.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neck: Carotids normal. Pulse documented as "no buits" in transcript; interpreted as no bruits.
Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, normal rate, crisp S1 and S2. No murmurs heard.
Respiratory: Lungs clear. No rales or wheezing.
Extremities: No edema. Pulses palpable at dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial. Thickened nails. Mildly dry skin. No skin breakdown.
Neurologic: Mildly decreased sensation in the tips of the first and second toes.

RESULTS
Recent A1c: 9.9 (per the doctor's statement; referenced from prior results).
Blood pressure: 140/60 in clinic (doctor's recheck). Home reading of 116 reported by patient, as noted above.
Labs: Blood work and kidney function to be checked today; results not available in the transcript.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes with poor control (A1c 9.9 per prior results, described by doctor as above 9): Increase glimepiride to 4 mg twice daily. Patient to take two 2 mg tablets twice daily until the new 4 mg prescription is filled, then one 4 mg tablet twice daily. Continue metformin. Recheck blood work today. Counsel on hypoglycemia symptoms. Reduce bread intake.
2. Hypertension: Continue metoprolol 50 mg daily, lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide 20/25 mg daily, and amlodipine 10 mg daily. Kidney function to be checked today.
3. Hyperlipidemia and peripheral vascular disease: Continue atorvastatin (high dose), per doctor, to protect the arteries.
4. Peripheral neuropathy (doctor's impression of foot symptoms): Keep feet moisturized. Medication an option if symptoms worsen; patient is already on many medications. Patient plans to obtain a foot cream or scrub.
5. Leg and hip pain: Possibly sciatica per doctor, not certain. Doctor describes symptoms as relatively stable. Patient to continue walking as tolerated.
6. Tobacco use: Advised to quit smoking. Patient not ready to quit at this time; states she will think about it.
7. Cataracts, status post surgery: Patient dissatisfied with one lens. Doctor suggested laser treatment may be possible, pending the eye provider's evaluation. Continue eye care with Optimum Optometrists (Dr. Sanchez previously seen).
8. Cough with congestion: Patient reports recent cough, improved this morning; lungs clear on exam.
9. Urinary symptoms: Slower stream, several daily voids, occasional nocturia. Patient attributes to age. No specific plan documented.

Follow-up: Return in four months. Labs drawn today.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up after emergency room visit for shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Louis is a 58-year-old male here for follow-up from an emergency room visit. On Saturday, while playing tennis in very hot, humid weather, he became very short of breath and was struggling to breathe after about half an hour. He thought he was having a heart attack and became very nervous. His wife took him to the emergency room, where everything checked out, but he was very upset about the episode. Approximately six hours after returning home, he felt very light-headed and dizzy. On Sunday he felt fine. He came in to have it checked.

The doctor wondered whether this might be heat exhaustion.

The patient reports taking all of his heart failure medications and being very diligent with them. He is in touch with his cardiologist and reports doing well apart from the episode on Saturday. He reports watching his diet and avoiding salty and junk food, but says he cheats every now and then and has had salty foods on occasion. He reports that for the most part he has been doing a good job.

Cataract removal was performed three months ago (on a Thursday), and he reports everything has been fine since then with no vision problems. Skin cancer was removed about five months ago, and the site healed nicely with no problems since.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for shortness of breath and light-headedness/dizziness (approximately six hours after the tennis episode), both related to the Saturday episode. Negative for vision problems. Otherwise not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure is elevated at today's visit. Blood pressure was also reported as high at the emergency room.
Neck: very supple; no jugular venous distention noted (transcribed as "fibular venous distention").
Cardiac: regular rate and rhythm, no murmur.
Lungs: fine crackles bilaterally.
Extremities: trace lower extremity edema in both legs.

RESULTS
ECG: Stable. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy, which the doctor stated caused his congestive heart failure.
Echocardiogram: Pumping function of the heart is a little low but stable.
Skin biopsy pathology: Reviewed; the doctor indicates all of the skin cancer was removed and everything is fine.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Shortness of breath at the emergency department, most likely an exacerbation of heart failure. The doctor's impression is that this was an exacerbation of heart failure, probably related to dietary indiscretion (eating salty food causing fluid retention). Exam findings of fine bilateral crackles and trace bilateral leg edema are consistent with extra fluid on board, per the doctor. Heat exhaustion was raised by the doctor as a possibility. Hypertension noted on today's visit and at the emergency room; the doctor plans to discuss this further with the patient.
   - Prescribe extra dose of Lasix (furosemide) 80 mg once daily.
   - Start carvedilol 25 mg twice daily.
2. Status post cataract removal: doing well, no vision problems; no medication changes needed per the doctor.
3. Status post skin cancer removal: healed well; pathology reviewed and everything fine; no medication changes needed per the doctor.
4. Nurse to see the patient shortly.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lower back injury, approximately four months ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Elevated and fluctuating blood pressure.

Mr. Thompson is a 67-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis who presents with elevated and fluctuating blood pressures. He describes feeling a little unsteady with the dizziness, and a slight headache when his readings are higher. He describes the dizziness as fuzzy lightheadedness rather than vertigo or spinning. He uses a pillbox and has also tried a phone app for medication tracking, which he found a little confusing, but reports he is largely on schedule. Osteoarthritis is managed with Tylenol as needed for mild pain and activity modification; he is still able to golf, though he sometimes plays less or skips a day with weather changes.

Positive: intermittent lightheadedness, slight headache with elevated readings, mild unsteadiness with dizziness, occasional chest heaviness, elevated home blood pressure readings.

Mostly normal and unremarkable overall.

Not discussed.

He is unsure whether he used proper lifting technique and states he probably did not. Pain is described as achy and sharp, localized to the low back. Initially it did not radiate, but he now feels it starting to shoot down the left leg. Sitting is usually tolerated. Patient reports the pain has been getting worse. He has taken ibuprofen and Tylenol, which sometimes helps. Patient reports no prior discussion of surgery; this is the first time it has been discussed. Patient exercises a few times a week but inconsistently and has a sedentary job. He reports the pain has not affected his job but he does not want to be as active as previously. Family history: father has back pain. Social history: does not smoke. Reports a history of playing soccer (midfield).

Negative: numbness, tingling, loss of sensation, weakness, loss of bladder or bowel control.

Not discussed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee pain after a twisting injury while water skiing.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports right knee pain that began about five days ago (last weekend) when he/she was water skiing on Lake Martin. While landing from a jump, the patient twisted the right knee. No pop was heard or felt; the patient described a sensation of something stretching, followed by swelling. The patient stated, "it might be a torn meniscus," but was not sure. The patient was able to exit the water unassisted but reported significant soreness with climbing, squatting, and bending. This is the first time the patient has injured this knee. Pain has been treated with over-the-counter Aleve twice daily and a cold pack, with a fair amount of relief, though the knee remains sore. The patient is a frequent water skier, going most weekends.

Hypertension: Patient reports taking lisinopril daily and checking home blood pressure, which has been about 125/80 on most days. Patient reports no side effects from lisinopril.

Patient denies numbness or tingling in the foot since the injury; reports only swelling and pain.

Surgical history: Tonsillectomy. No other surgeries found in the record.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for right knee pain and swelling. Negative for numbness or tingling in the right foot. No lisinopril side effects reported.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure about 120/70 in the office; patient was likely in some pain at the time of measurement.
Neck: No lymphadenopathy appreciated.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur appreciated.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal, right knee: Ecchymosis and edema present. Effusion present. Pain to palpation of the right medial knee. Decreased range of motion. Negative varus and valgus stress tests. Negative Lachman sign.
Lower extremity vascular: Palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. No other lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right knee pain with medial collateral ligament strain (per doctor's assessment). Right knee effusion and inflammation noted on exam. The doctor believes this is a medial collateral ligament strain and does not think a fracture is present, but ordered an X-ray of the right knee to rule out broken bones. The doctor noted that this injury typically heals well without surgery. Plan: right knee X-ray; physical therapy referral to strengthen muscles around the knee; meloxicam 15 mg by mouth once daily for swelling and pain. The doctor advised the patient to rest the knee and avoid skiing for now, citing the risk of further injury if the patient falls, at least until X-ray results are available. The patient's question about skiing tomorrow was addressed with this advice. The patient's concern about a torn meniscus was mentioned by the patient; the doctor's examination findings did not specifically address meniscal injury in the transcript.

2. Hypertension. Blood pressure controlled per patient home readings and office measurement. Plan: continue lisinopril 20 mg daily; order lipid panel.

3. Health maintenance. Tetanus vaccination due per health record; tetanus shot to be given at this visit.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Cough, with worsening over the last two days. Right knee pain after a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 74-year-old male teacher with a history of hypertension and diabetes who presents with a cough that started about one week ago. He reports bringing up yellow sputum. He feels worse over the last two days. He states he thinks it could be the flu; this is the patient's impression. He feels warm but has not checked his temperature. He reports some chills absent and mild intermittent achiness. He denies shortness of breath. He reports nasal congestion, postnasal drainage down the throat, and some sinus pressure. No one else in his household is sick.

Right knee injury: While coughing earlier today, he fell down four or five stairs and injured his right knee. He has been able to walk since the injury, with pain mostly on the medial (inside) aspect and a mild limp. He reports he can bend and straighten the knee and that it does not feel like it will give out. He has taken over-the-counter cough and cold medication (DayQuil), which has helped the cough a little. He has not taken other pain medication.

Hypertension: He has a history of hypertension that has been difficult to control over the past year. He has not obtained a blood pressure cuff as previously requested and does not check his blood pressure at home. He reports taking lisinopril, which he believes is 20 mg daily, and states it is a white pill. He is not monitoring his salt intake and states he feels the blood pressure medicine will do what it is supposed to do.

Diabetes: He is not monitoring his sugar intake and does not check his blood sugars. He reports taking metformin, which he believes is the large pill, and states his wife fills his pill box and he takes medication twice daily. The prescribed dose discussed by the doctor is 1000 mg twice daily; the patient confirms he takes it twice daily.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Feels warm, no reported chills, mild intermittent achiness. No fever measured at home.
Respiratory: Productive cough with yellow sputum, no shortness of breath.
HEENT: Nasal congestion, postnasal drainage, sinus pressure.
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, medial, with mild limp.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Temperature 98.4. Blood pressure approximately 125/62. Heart rate in the 80s, regular. Oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
HEENT: Pain to palpation of bilateral maxillary sinuses. Erythema and edema of bilateral nasal turbinates with associated yellow discharge. Throat: uvula midline, no erythema, edema, or exudate in the peritonsillar space.
Neck: Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
Lungs: Coarse rhonchi bilaterally that clear with cough.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur appreciated.
Right knee: Pain to palpation. Decreased flexion and extension. Ecchymosis to the right medial knee. No evidence of effusion.

RESULTS
No laboratory or imaging results were available at the time of the visit. Right knee x-ray and chest x-ray (if indicated) were discussed as orders; no results reported. Lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c were ordered; no results reported.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Cough with upper respiratory symptoms, likely viral syndrome with probable mild bronchitis (doctor's assessment). Findings consistent with mild upper respiratory infection with congestion. Plan: supportive care, continue over-the-counter medications, guaifenesin 600 mg twice daily. No antibiotics at this time. Call if symptoms worsen; chest x-ray to be considered if worsening to rule out pneumonia.

2. Right knee pain after fall, suspected right medial collateral ligament strain (doctor's assessment). Plan: meloxicam 15 mg once daily, referral to physical therapy, right knee x-ray to rule out bony injury (doctor does not think a fracture is present).

3. Hypertension, reported suboptimal home monitoring; office blood pressure approximately 125/62. Plan: continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, order lipid panel. Patient to obtain home blood pressure monitoring as previously requested.

4. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (diabetes type not specified in transcript), not monitoring blood sugars or diet. Plan: order hemoglobin A1c to assess need for metformin adjustment; continue metformin as prescribed; monitor sugar intake and report blood sugars through the patient portal. Doctor counseled on the risks of diabetes complications, including kidney dysfunction and eye problems.

Patient agreed with the plan and will follow up with results communicated by the doctor.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right upper abdominal pain for several weeks, referred by Dr. Miller after abdominal ultrasound showed gallstones.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a diabetic male (described by the doctor as type 2 diabetes, managed with diet and exercise) who reports several weeks of pain on the right side of the abdomen, right underneath the ribs. He describes the pain as squeezing and severe, coming and going, and rates severe episodes as 8 out of 10. He reports associated nausea and sick feeling in the stomach. He has not vomited. He reports low-grade fevers during periods when the pain is severe, lasting a couple of days. Pain usually occurs immediately after eating or a couple of hours after eating. He states he thinks it could be a stomach ulcer; this is the patient's own suspicion and was not evaluated in the transcript.

Dietary history: He reports he previously had a worse diet before diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. Since then he has cut back on sugar, started a keto diet, and reports about a 25-pound weight loss over the last three months. He reports his blood sugars are improving. He has cut out pork rinds (pork grinds), which he previously ate as a staple, and reports his pain is somewhat better but still present.

Family history: Both his father and mother had gallbladder disease and required cholecystectomy.

Activity: He reports he has not been significantly limited in exercise, though he usually watches his timing around meals. He enjoys outdoor photography and plans to get out more this spring.

Prior workup: Per the patient, Dr. Miller performed an abdominal ultrasound and diagnosed gallstones, and recommended dietary avoidance of high-fat foods. Pain persists despite these changes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for right upper abdominal pain, nausea, and subjective low-grade fevers during painful episodes. Negative for vomiting per the patient.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/88, respiratory rate 16, pulse 68, afebrile today, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No ectopic beats. No clicks, rubs, or murmurs noted.
Respiratory: Lungs clear and equal bilaterally to auscultation.
Abdomen: Positive bowel sounds. Soft, nondistended. Slight guarding in the right upper quadrant. No rebound tenderness. Positive Murphy's sign with tenderness on palpation beneath the right ribs on inspiration. No peritoneal signs appreciated.

RESULTS
Abdominal ultrasound (reviewed by the doctor): Multiple gallstones present in the gallbladder. Mild gallbladder wall thickening. Common bile duct within normal limits at 4.1 mm. No frank obstruction appreciated on doctor's assessment.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Mild cholecystitis with gallstones, per the doctor's assessment. The doctor notes no frank obstruction and suspects the gallbladder inflammation developed over the last few weeks. Because symptoms have not improved with dietary modification, the doctor recommends laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Procedure explained: small incisions, laparoscopic removal of the gallbladder, estimated 1 to 1.5 hours. Expected overnight hospital stay for monitoring. Continue avoiding high-fat foods after surgery and eat a high-fiber diet. The patient had no questions about the plan.
   - Postoperative activity: take it easy for the first 24 hours; walk on solid ground within a day or two; no hiking initially; follow-up in about one week for release to full activity.
2. Type 2 diabetes, managed with diet and exercise. Per the doctor, the patient should follow up with his primary care provider or endocrinologist regarding diabetes management in light of upcoming surgery. Glycemic monitoring to continue per those providers.
3. Paperwork: nurse to obtain signatures on consent/paperwork.
4. Follow-up: return next week to proceed with surgery.

He has cut out pork rinds, which were a staple of his keto diet, and reports his pain is somewhat better but still present.

Family history: Both his father and mother had gallbladder disease and required cholecystectomy.

Activity: He reports he is not significantly limited in exercise. He has never been a big exerciser immediately after eating. He enjoys nature photography and plans to start photographing outdoors now that spring has arrived.

COVID-19 test performed today per patient agreement; result not yet available in transcript. Results to be given to patient.

Routine follow-up of chronic problems (depression, asthma, diabetes).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Joseph is a 59-year-old male here for routine follow-up of chronic problems. He reports he has been managing through his depression, and his asthma has been acting up due to a bad pollen season. He states he is at least keeping his diabetes under control, though he describes persistent issues overall.

Diabetes: He reports his diet has been good for the most part, but during a weekend of travel to children's sports tournaments he ate on the go, including junk food and pizza, and did not stick to his diet.

Asthma: He uses his inhaler only when temperatures go above about 85 degrees Fahrenheit, which is when he feels it most. On cool, dry days he does not use the inhaler. He exercises in the morning, riding a bike for about 45 minutes.

Depression: He was taking prozac 20 mg daily regularly but has weaned himself off of it. He felt a little better but states he goes through battles with depression every so often. He is willing to try something different, and would consider adjusting his current medication to a lower dose to reduce side effects, or switching medications.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional/Cardiovascular: While running up and down stairs in warm weather, he felt lightheaded and dizzy; he attributed this to heat and fatigue. The doctor stated that this could be low blood sugar.
Respiratory: Shortness of breath with exertion (stairs). No fever or chills were reported in the transcript.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain.
Musculoskeletal: Mild knee pain from running up and down and picking up boxes; he describes nothing out of the ordinary.
Chest pain: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: In no apparent distress.
Neck: No cervical lymphadenopathy. Thyroid not enlarged.
Respiratory: Faint bilateral expiratory wheezing.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Abdomen: Soft.
Extremities: No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs): Reviewed by the doctor; described as looking quite good.
Hemoglobin A1c: Reviewed by the doctor; per the doctor, blood sugar has probably been running a little high over the past couple of months.
Chest x-ray: Reviewed by the doctor; looks fine, with no pneumonia. The doctor stated the findings are all from asthma.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Type 2 diabetes (as referenced in transcript as diabetes): Hemoglobin A1c suggests blood sugar has probably been running a little high over the past couple of months, per the doctor. CHIEF COMPLAINT
Back pain following a golf injury, approximately four days duration.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
James is a 57-year-old male with a past medical history significant for congestive heart failure and type 2 diabetes who presents with back pain. He reports that on Saturday morning, about four days ago, he was golfing and injured his back during his backswing. He felt a pop and immediately had to go to the ground. Frequent asthma symptoms with cough and wheezing; patient frustrated that asthma does not seem to improve.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports ongoing cough and wheezing and feels her asthma is never controlled. She notes that when she gets a cold, her asthma almost always flares. She reports one prior flare after visiting her aunt's house, which she attributes to the aunt's cat; she avoids that house and has had no issue since. Per patient, symptoms occur every month or every other month over the past six months. She has been seen at urgent care and by her primary care provider, where she has received antibiotics at times and steroids at other times. Once, the flare was severe enough that she went to the emergency department. Patient describes that urgent care and ED visits almost always include a prednisone course, sometimes a large dose over five days and sometimes a tapering course over nine to ten days. Last exacerbation was about one month ago per patient.

Patient uses two inhalers but reports only one helps; she identifies the helpful one as a blue inhaler, which she named as Ventolin (albuterol). She reports using it almost daily because of cough and wheezing, and waking at night a couple of times a night some nights and a couple of times a week on others, with relief after two puffs, usually enough to return to sleep. Patient reports one prior hospitalization at about age eight for asthma; none since.

Patient denies seasonal allergies. She enjoys hiking and is looking forward to hiking the new trails behind the Wreck Center once her symptoms improve, while being careful given her cough and wheeze. Patient denies current or past smoking, vaping/e-cigarette use, and regular marijuana use. She reports occasionally going to bars with friends, where smoke irritates her; she tries not to go often.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for cough, wheezing, and nocturnal awakenings with asthma symptoms. Negative for seasonal allergies per patient. Other systems not discussed.

Vitals reviewed: blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No ectopy appreciated. No rubs, murmurs, or gallops.
Respiratory: Diminished breath sounds throughout with occasional slight expiratory wheeze, bilateral.
Neck: Supple. Trachea midline. No lymphadenopathy. No carotid bruit.
Extremities: Strong bilateral pulses. No clubbing. Brisk capillary refill.

RESULTS
Pulmonary function testing performed at today's visit reviewed by the doctor; results described as consistent with asthma. No specific values were stated in the transcript.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Asthma, moderate intermittent (per doctor's assessment). Doctor states symptoms are consistent with moderate intermittent asthma.
- Start Flovent (fluticasone) 110 micrograms, one puff twice daily, with emphasis on consistent use to help prevent daily symptoms and reduce reliance on rescue inhaler.

- Patient's cat exposure at aunt's house noted as a likely trigger per patient's report.
- Follow-up in one month, or sooner if symptoms worsen.
- Patient agreed with the plan.

Non-healing wound on the right foot for approximately two to three weeks.

He previously saw a podiatrist a couple of years ago but was unable to establish care with another podiatrist after that practice moved. The wound has been present for about two to three weeks. It began as a blister after he bought a new pair of shoes to travel with. Patient stated he did not feel the shoes were too tight at first. He reports that the neuropathy may have contributed to not noticing the tightness, though he stated this with uncertainty ("I guess"). He has been covering the wound with a band-aid. He reports the wound looked about the same after the course. He denies pain and states he cannot feel it. He reports the sock sometimes sticks to the wound when removed, even with a band-aid in place. Patient denies any trauma other than the new shoes. The shoes are Hoka brand, purchased at REI a couple of years ago. Patient describes them as comfortable, easy to take on and off, and providing good stability. Patient reports he has had some issues with stability at times. Patient reports his diabetes is "not too bad," with a most recent hemoglobin A1c "a little over eight" per his report.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever and chills.
Skin: Denies drainage from the wound. Reports sock sticking to the wound.
Neurologic: Reports neuropathy. Denies pain in the foot.
Musculoskeletal: Reports some stability issues at times.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right foot pain following a tennis injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a right-handed adult female (named Brittany in the transcript) who presents with right foot pain after an injury approximately a couple of days ago while playing doubles tennis. While attempting to volley, she got in front of another player and fell on top of her foot. She then twisted to try to catch herself and felt pain in the foot. The patient stated she thinks it could be a bone bruise. She was unable to continue playing and had to be helped off the field because she could not bear weight on the foot. Since the injury she has wrapped the foot with elastic wraps, iced it, elevated it on a pillow, and taken ibuprofen, which helps a little but wears off after a while. She denies numbness. She reports she can still feel her foot. She has previously injured her left foot; she has not previously injured the right foot.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for numbness. No loss of sensation reported.
Otherwise, Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Blood pressure 125/70. Respiratory rate 18. Temperature 97.1. Oxygen saturation 100%. Pulse approximately 60 beats per minute. Per the doctor, vitals look great.
Cardiac: No murmur, rub, or gallop. Regular rate and rhythm.
Respiratory: Doctor appreciates a little bit of stridor. No wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: No rebound. No guarding.
Skin: Doctor reports no feeling of heat on touch. Head appears symmetrical. Mucous membranes normal.
Right foot: Bruising of the plantar and dorsal aspects of the foot. Associated swelling. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot. Patient denies pain on palpation of the midfoot at one point in the exam. Positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. Warm to touch.
Right foot neurovascular: Capillary refill less than 3 seconds. Strong dorsalis pedis pulse. Sensation intact to light touch.
Left foot: Normal. Capillary refill appropriate, pedal pulses strong, sensation intact.

RESULTS
Right foot X-ray (reviewed by the doctor): Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal. Three millimeter separation of the first and second metatarsal bases. Presence of a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture involving the second metatarsal base, per the doctor's assessment based on exam and X-ray.
- Doctor recommends surgery to place bones in proper position using plates and screws to help prevent further complications. Doctor states that without surgery there can be significant complications, including poor bone alignment, poor ligament healing, loss of the arch (flat foot), and arthritis. Patient asked whether surgery is required; doctor highly recommends it.
- Doctor will order an MRI to further assess the fracture and any ligament injury.
- Surgery is described as a day procedure with same-day discharge. Patient will need a driver to take her home. Follow-up in the clinic in about one week. Cast and crutches; non-weight-bearing on the right foot for six to eight weeks, then gradual weight-bearing as tolerated based on progress.
- Patient is out for the rest of the tennis season per the doctor. Patient expressed a desire to return to play.
- Physical therapy recommended after surgery to strengthen muscles and prepare for return to play.
- Surgical risks, including bleeding, loss of sensation, and nerve damage, to be reviewed; paperwork to be provided and reviewed by the medical assistant. Patient instructed to ask questions before and after the procedure.

Follow-up after inferior STEMI with stent placement. Patient reported chest pain prior to emergency room evaluation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient has a history of RCA stent placed in 2018 and has been followed by this physician since then. She presents for follow-up after an inferior STEMI, for which another stent was placed. She reports that she developed severe chest pain that did not resolve, prompting an emergency room visit, where she was told she needed another stent. She describes the episode as similar to her prior heart attack. The doctor suggested the chest pain might be acid reflux, stating uncertainty ("it might be acid reflux, I'm not sure").

Since her last visit about six months ago, the patient reports she has been doing fine and walks her dog daily for about one and a half to two miles. She reports new leg swelling since discharge from the hospital. She states she sleeps on a couple of pillows and has needed to sit up somewhat more at night, but she feels this is mostly normal. She reports she can afford her medications, has good insurance, and is taking them as prescribed.

Diet: Patient reports she has not strictly adjusted her salt intake, having become less strict since her last heart attack. She states she will need to resume salt restriction. She reports eating pizza with occasional pepperoni and vegetables.

Diabetes: Patient reports monitoring her blood sugars and taking metformin, and she wishes to avoid insulin. She states she is trying to stay active.

Known history: coronary artery disease, hypertension, and diabetes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: bilateral leg swelling since hospital discharge; increased need to sit up at night (patient feels this is mostly normal).
Negative: chest pain and shortness of breath were asked about; the patient's answer did not directly address these symptoms and was not clearly documented as negative. Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Described by the doctor as good.
Neck: No jugular venous distention. No carotid bruits.
Cardiac: Three out of six systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base.
Lungs: Clear.
Extremities: Lower limb edema, pitting one plus. Right radial artery pulses palpable. Right radial catheterization site clean, dry, and intact without hematoma.

RESULTS
ECG: Normal sinus rhythm, good R wave progression, and evolutionary changes anticipated after STEMI.
Echocardiogram: Reduced ejection fraction of 35 percent.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Coronary artery disease (primary diagnosis, established history):
- Continue aspirin 81 mg daily and Brilinta 90 mg twice daily.
- Continue high-dose statin (Lipitor) 80 mg daily.
- Continue Toprol 50 mg daily.
- Referral to cardiac rehabilitation for education and exercise confidence.
- Continued evaluation over time.

2. Newly reduced left ventricular systolic function and moderate mitral regurgitation:
- Doctor's opinion: the reduced pumping function is concerning but is likely to improve over time given her history and rapid cath lab intervention; the doctor believes the myocardium may be stunned and that she will recover, given medication adherence.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.

3. Acute heart failure (doctor's assessment, based on fluid retention):
- Start Lasix (furosemide) 40 mg once daily.
- Add Aldactone (spironolactone) 12.5 mg daily.
- Labs to be obtained.
- Repeat echocardiogram in about two months.

4. Hypertension:
- Blood pressure described by the doctor as fine. Doctor expects the patient to tolerate Aldactone well.
- Referral to nutrition counseling to discuss dietary options, including reducing preserved meats such as pepperoni and finding alternatives.

Patient agreed with the plan, stating she will work on her diet and expressed belief that she will get better. Doctor expressed strong belief that this is the best course and that the patient will improve with time, and will monitor over time.

New right eye twitch, noticed by father for a couple of weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Karen Nelson is a 3-year-old female with no significant past medical history who presents with her father for evaluation of a new right eye twitch. Father noticed the twitch a couple of weeks ago and was advised by the pediatrician to come in for evaluation. Father stated that the twitch occurs several times an hour on some days, and on other days is not seen until late afternoon; he has noticed it every day for the last several weeks. Karen reports feeling the twitch in her face at times. She reports no pain with the twitch. She describes an urge to move her face, after which the movement occurs and she feels better. Father describes the whole side of her face moving during an episode, lasting several seconds, after which it stops and she appears to blink frequently. Karen continues her usual activities during episodes. Father reports she is eating well, playing with friends, and otherwise acting normally, and states she seems fine. Father stated that he made a video of the episode, which was offered for review. No history of seizures in Karen or in the family. No family history of Tourette syndrome per father. No movements or twitching of other body parts noted by father.

Doctor's initial impression, stated during the visit: possibly allergies.

Father was advised to review the video of the episode, which was offered for review by the doctor.

Doctor suggested a possible hiatal hernia as a consideration; this was the doctor's impression and was not confirmed in the transcript.

Diet and social history: Over the last couple of months, patient reports increased stress related to a move across the country. During this period he has been drinking more and eating foods such as pizza and burgers, which he acknowledges are not good for him. He has not lost weight and reports unintentional weight gain.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain, swelling, and limited motion following a hyperextension injury sustained in a motor vehicle accident in March of this year. Patient presents for a second opinion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 50-year-old right-handed male (date of birth 1/12/71) who was a passenger in a car that was rear-ended multiple times in March of this year. He felt two bumps that threw him forward and caused him to stretch out his right index finger. He is not certain whether the finger was dislocated. He felt that the finger was laid upon and that it went backward. He has had pain since March, with persistent swelling. He is unable to make a fist, and at times the pain is unbearable. Driving hurts.

Prior care: He was seen at Point May Orthopedics, where he was largely managed by physical therapy staff and a PR/PA. He was offered an injection of the A1 pulley region but declined steroid because of a reaction to dexamethasone, which he reports causes his heart to race. He was scheduled to see Dr. Alice Davis, which the doctor noted does not appear to have occurred. Per the doctor, there was concern for a capsular strain plus or minus rupture of the "FDS tendon." Per the patient, he was told the MRI showed a tear and that he would not receive an injection because it could worsen the tear, and later was told he would be offered an injection but no surgery. He reports occupational therapy has advised him not to keep rubbing the finger or using the hand for tasks, and he feels he is not receiving adequate medical care. He reports a prior reaction to methylprednisolone with itching.

Occupation: X-ray technician.

Medications: Blood pressure medication. No chronic medications of significance otherwise discussed.

Comorbidities: Patient denies diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.

Patient came to seek treatment to improve function of the right hand, which he needs for work.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for right index finger pain, swelling, stiffness, and numbness over the finger when pressed. Positive for itching with prior methylprednisolone. Negative for diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis per patient. Other systems not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Well-appearing, pleasant, cooperative, healthy-appearing male in no distress. Heart rate regular rate and rhythm. Radial pulse 2+. No swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases. Slightly diminished over the PIP joint of the index finger compared with the middle finger. Index finger rests in a 10-degree PIP flexed position. Tenderness with pressure over the index finger region; less tender at a second site. Patient reports a little numbness. Active flexion testing of the index finger was performed; patient reports a sensation of tearing with forceful flexion and pain with flexion at the MCP region. Patient reports pain with the maneuver described as the MCP flexion.

RESULTS
Prior MRI of the right index finger, 4/24/2021 (per outside practice, as reported): focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint; partial-thickness tear of the right FDS; fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact, as is the MCP joint capsule. Extensor tendons intact.

X-rays, four views of the right hand, today: no bony abnormalities; joint congruency throughout all lesser digits of the right hand; no concerning soft tissue shadows; no arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Post-traumatic, rather severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger, per the doctor. Doctor's opinion: there is a partial tear in one half of the FDS tendon, which the doctor describes as the less important of the two flexor tendons; the FDP, which extends to the fingertip, is intact. Doctor's opinion: scar tissue and inflammation around the FDS are blocking excursion of the other tendons so they cannot pass through the pulley. Doctor's opinion: the injury is post-traumatic with post-traumatic inflammation and scar tissue; the extensor tendons and collateral ligaments are intact, so there is no expected risk of tearing or breaking a bone with movement, though the finger is stiff and sore.

Plan:
1. Right index finger trigger finger injection with betamethasone (Celestone), 1 cc, with lidocaine, as the doctor's chosen steroid, avoiding dexamethasone per the doctor because of the patient's reaction to it. Doctor expects pain relief within 3 to 5 days and further improvement over the following couple of weeks; repeat injection may be needed.
2. Outpatient occupational/physical therapy once weekly for six weeks, with the goal of full active and passive range of motion without restrictions. Patient to check in weekly for accountability. Patient to return to his prior therapy providers, with the doctor hoping he will progress after the injection.
3. Patient instructed to actively move the finger; splint use discouraged by the doctor because it immobilizes the finger.
4. Driving reported as safe by the doctor.
5. Procedure note: The first attempt at injection with 1 cc Celestone and 0.5 cc lidocaine was aborted after the patient had a dramatic, violent painful reaction to needle introduction, with hand contortions and forceful withdrawal, raising concern for secondary needle stick; the needle was withdrawn. The patient was counseled on the importance of getting therapeutic steroid into the flexor tendon sheath. A second attempt with the same technique and medication was performed. A small palmar vein bled a scant amount, which was cleaned and a bandage applied. The patient was reassured repeatedly that no harm was done to the finger. Post-procedure recommendations: icing the finger this evening and taking ibuprofen.

New patient visit, referred by primary care physician Dr. Scott
Provider: Dr. Phillips

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Acid reflux. Referred by primary care physician Dr. Scott.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports severe acid reflux. She has had reflux since about age 12, with worsening over the past few years. She currently takes omeprazole 40 mg twice daily for about one year. Symptoms are fine on some days and severe on others. She describes burning in the chest and throat. She reports that omeprazole has helped, but symptoms still flare, especially after eating. She reports that her symptoms are worsened by spicy foods, carbonated beverages (including soda), tomato-based foods, and citrus, and sometimes by stress and food choices. She says she tries to avoid spicy foods and soda but still eats tomato and citrus products sometimes. She reports decreased appetite for the past two months and high work stress. She describes her weight as pretty stable.

Surgical history: abdominal surgery in infancy, at about one month of age, for intestinal twisting per patient's mother. Patient is unsure of the exact details.
Prior endoscopy: possibly an upper endoscopy in childhood. None in the last 10 years.
Medication history: omeprazole and ranitidine in the past. Ranitidine helped. These are the only medications she has taken for this problem.
Family history: maternal grandmother had esophageal cancer. Mother had acid reflux and took a medication that coats the stomach lining.
Occupation: paralegal.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive: heartburn and burning in the chest and throat, decreased appetite for about two months, work-related stress and anxiety.
Negative: dysphagia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel habits, constipation, diarrhea, rectal bleeding.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Heart and lungs auscultated. Per the physician's new patient template, the exam was otherwise normal. Well-healed abdominal surgical scars were noted.

RESULTS
Not discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), several-year history, poorly controlled on omeprazole 40 mg twice daily. Patient reports ongoing heartburn despite the medication.
The physician suspects GERD with an underlying functional etiology as well. This is the physician's clinical impression, not a confirmed diagnosis. The physician also raised the possibility of a hiatal hernia, stating uncertainty.
Patient reports no unintentional weight loss, though she reports decreased appetite for two months. She denies dysphagia.

- Dietary modification: avoid trigger foods, including spicy foods, carbonated beverages, citrus, and tomato-based products. The physician advised that these can worsen GERD even while on a PPI. Patient agrees to improve avoidance.

- Contingency plan (physician): if the EGD is normal and symptoms persist despite a trial of Nexium, consider a trial of Protonix and a pH-impedance study. The physician stated this would rule out abnormal acid reflux exposure and help distinguish a functional etiology from hypersensitivity.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Yearly follow-up for asthma, allergic rhinitis, and food allergy (peanut allergy).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 20-year-old female (DOB March 26, 2001) seen for yearly follow-up. Last office visit was in April 2020; last contact was a telemedicine visit a little over a year ago. Due to insurance changes, she was switched from Symbicort to Wixela 250/50 and reports it is working well. She uses one puff in the morning and one puff at night, but has been taking it less often; she estimates she takes both doses about three to four days per week and once daily on other days. She states she sometimes feels she does not need it. She reports she is trying to reduce use because she intends to enlist in the military, expected early spring 2022, and wants to show she can meet fitness requirements without an inhaler. She uses albuterol rarely, mainly before strenuous exertion such as running, and uses it as a preventive before exertion. She reports no urgent care or ED visits for breathing over the past year and no prednisone courses for breathing issues.

Patient stated, "it might be vocal cord dysfunction, i'm not sure." This was the patient's own suspicion; the doctor did not comment on it in the transcript.

Allergic rhinitis: Patient uses Zyrtec (cetirizine) during spring and fall, and as needed in summer, mainly on days she expects to be outside (she works outside about three days per week). She reports it works well.

Peanut allergy: Patient has a known peanut allergy. Last year she developed hives after cleaning out a rental car (Enterprise) that contained peanuts and touching it. She reports no reactions since, and wears long sleeves and changes gloves when cleaning cars. She notes airplanes serve peanuts. She carries an EpiPen and needs refills. She tolerates almonds and cashews per the doctor's note; she recalls eating almonds previously without reaction but usually avoids tree nuts.

Tobacco/vaping: Patient reports she developed a habit of vaping and smoking over the past year, has been trying to cut back, and now uses only a little and is trying to quit. The doctor noted this can affect breathing test results.

Interval history: Written consent was obtained today to use DAX for documentation.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Respiratory: Denies urgent care or ED visits for breathing over the past year and no prednisone use. Reports rare albuterol use with strenuous activity.
Allergic: Seasonal allergy symptoms well controlled with Zyrtec. No reactions to peanut exposure since the prior episode.
Other systems: Not discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Ears: Normal, with a little wax bilaterally.
Oral cavity: Examined; no findings documented.
Nose: Examined; no findings documented.
Lungs: Clear with good air movement; "sound terrific" per doctor.
Heart: Listened to; no findings documented beyond "very good."

RESULTS
Spirometry (breathing test) completed today: Results are about the same as a couple of years ago and look a little better. Doctor noted prior test in 2019 was likely lower due to smoke from wildfires at that time. Patient reports she was feeling poorly then due to smoke.
Asthma Control Test (ACT) score: 21.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Asthma
- Spirometry is about the same as prior and slightly improved. Doctor attributes the prior lower 2019 numbers to wildfire smoke exposure.
- Doctor stated that current guidelines recommend considering using inhaled steroid/combination therapy only during illness or smoke season, rather than year-round, and that this could be a possibility if the patient does well; the doctor noted that more frequent symptoms each month would indicate too little reduction.
- Options discussed: (1) continue Wixela off-label once daily; (2) step down to Alvesco, which Kaiser covers. Doctor recommended starting with Alvesco.
- Plan: Prescribe Alvesco 80 mcg, two puffs twice daily, sent to Kaiser Permanente Broadway pharmacy. Patient to set aside Wixela but not discard it in case Alvesco is ineffective.
- Renew albuterol as needed.
- Repeat spirometry and ACT in four months; sooner if needed. Military may require documentation of breathing tests.

2. Allergic rhinitis
- Continue Zyrtec (cetirizine) 10 mg as needed, over the counter.

3. Peanut allergy (tree nut avoidance)
- Continue strict avoidance of peanuts and tree nuts.
- Renew EpiPen.
- Doctor noted that many people with peanut allergy also avoid tree nuts; patient tolerates almonds and cashews per doctor's note, but patient usually avoids tree nuts.

4. Nebulizer
- Patient reports no current need for refills; last use was during bronchitis and childhood.

5. Tobacco and vaping use
- Patient reports attempting to quit; doctor noted this may affect breathing test results.

Follow-up: Four months with ACT and spirometry, sooner if needed. Follow-up visit time noted as 25 minutes.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Back pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
John is a 61-year-old male with a past medical history significant for kidney stones, migraines, and reflux who presents with back pain. Per the doctor's introduction, the patient has a history of kidney stones, migraines, and reflux.

The patient reports back pain similar to the pain he had with kidney stones about two years ago, and he is concerned about this. The pain started on the right side of his back and has shifted to the left side. He reports the pain has been present for the last four days. Initially the pain came and went; for about the last 48 hours it has been constant and pretty bad. He has taken Tylenol without significant relief.

The patient thinks he may have blood in his urine; he describes it as hard to detect but looking a little off-color. He reports that with exertion, such as climbing three flights of stairs or running to catch the bus, he feels a little dizzy and light-headed and still has more pain in his abdomen. Nausea and vomiting were asked about; the transcript does not document the patient's specific answer to nausea or vomiting.

The doctor suggested that the back pain could be a pulled muscle. The doctor later assessed that the patient is having a recurrence of his kidney stones.

Migraines: The patient was started on Imitrex a couple of months ago and reports being diligent with medication. He reports no migraine issues.

Reflux: The patient reports good adherence to dietary changes overall, but since the onset of pain he has been ordering more take-out and fast food for delivery to avoid the stairs. He reports he is staying hydrated.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for back pain, dizziness (with exertion), possible blood in urine, and abdominal pain with exertion. Patient reports body aches, which he attributes to favoring his back when walking, and notes they feel muscular but are not out of the ordinary and are similar to his prior episode two years ago. Negative for migraine issues. Patient reports he is staying hydrated. Chest pain was asked about; the transcript does not document a specific answer.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure is a little high today, which the doctor attributed probably to pain.
Cardiac and pulmonary: Heart sounds clear. Lungs clear.
Back: Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness on the right side.
Abdomen: Tenderness to palpation of the right lower quadrant.

RESULTS
Creatinine: Drawn today due to concern for kidney stones; slightly elevated. The doctor noted this might suggest a partial obstruction from a stone.
Abdominal x-rays: Show a possible kidney stone. A possible stone may be present lower down; the official radiology read is pending.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Back pain: The doctor thinks the patient is having a recurrence of kidney stones.
   - Order CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast.
   - Order Ultram 50 mg every six hours as needed for pain.
   - Push fluids and strain urine.
   - Nurse to help schedule the CT scan.
   - The doctor will follow up with the patient in about a day.
   - Patient to call if symptoms worsen.
2. Migraines: Continue Imitrex.
3. Reflux: Continue Protonix 40 mg daily; refill ordered.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Numbness and tingling in both hands for a few weeks. Referred for evaluation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 60-year-old right-handed male (MRN abc123, DOB January 1, 1960) referred for evaluation of numbness and tingling in both hands for a few weeks. Patient attributes the onset to a car accident last December in which he broke both wrists. He noticed the tingling and numbness more once the wrists healed. The right wrist was more severely affected at the time of injury. Patient wears a splint on the right wrist and sometimes on the left; the splint helps the right. Symptoms have worsened in both hands over the last month.

Patient reports mild neck stiffness and states he hit his head during the accident, and was told he had a contusion.

Location: Patient describes the right-side symptoms as involving the middle and ring fingers, extending up the forearm. Left-side symptoms involve the pinky and ring fingers, as described by the doctor during the visit.

Character: Mainly soreness, sometimes throbbing. Patient feels the hands are weaker, especially with use. Tingling is more pronounced when the hands hurt; when it resolves, the tingling is dull.

Timing: Symptoms are worse at night and come and go throughout the day.

Sensation: Patient does not recall loss of light touch but feels the hands may be less sensitive than expected, though he can still feel.

Medications: Prescribed nerve pain medication, which patient has not been taking as directed. Patient is taking coreg for hypertension and lexapro for anxiety.

Past history: Prediabetes, reported as controlled through diet. No history of thyroid disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Reviewed by doctor and confirmed by patient as correct:
Constitutional: fatigue, weight gain.
GI: excessive appetite, bloating.
Eyes: floaters.
Cardiovascular: shortness of breath, leg swelling.
Endocrine: always hungry.
Skin: nail bed changes, dryness, itching.
Musculoskeletal: gout, muscle pain.
All other systems reviewed and negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Neurologic examination:
Sensation: Normal to light touch in the right hand, with patient reporting slightly less sensation in two fingers. Pin prick diminished in the right third and fourth fingers. Left hand: patient reports decreased sensation in two fingers; pin prick decreased in the left fourth and fifth fingers. Doctor's documented findings are as stated.
Reflexes: 1+ and symmetric. Knee reflexes 2+. Toes downgoing bilaterally.
Tinel sign: positive at both wrists and both elbows, with patient reporting a zing up the wrist and into the elbow on both sides.
Remainder of exam documented as normal.

RESULTS
No laboratory or imaging results discussed. EMG has been ordered and is pending.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Assessment: Doctor states that what is seen today is bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. Doctor also notes that bilateral cubital tunnel syndrome is a possibility. Doctor's opinion is that the symptom presentation suggests bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, with the nerves at the wrists aggravated by past trauma, causing the pain and tingling.

Plan:
1. EMG nerve conduction study to localize the nerve irritation and assess nerve responsiveness.
2. Continue wearing splints.
3. Follow-up visit after testing is completed.
4. If symptoms persist, consider referral to the hand clinic for possible injections or carpal tunnel release surgery, or referral to an orthopedist for the same treatment.
5. Patient to resume the prescribed nerve pain medication as directed. (Note: the transcript records that the patient has not been taking it as prescribed; no new instruction was documented.)

Patient agreed with the plan.

Annual exam. Follow-up of congestive heart failure, depression, and hypertension.

Congestive heart failure: She reports good adherence to a low-sodium diet and states she has resisted salty foods. She reports taking her medications. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, and leg swelling that she has noticed.

Depression: She reports she has been attending therapy weekly for the past year and that it has helped a lot. She denies thoughts of harming herself or others. The doctor noted the patient was previously kept off medication for depression because she takes medications for her other problems.

Hypertension: She reports she continues to forget to take her blood pressure medications. She notes her blood pressure rises when work becomes more stressful. Work has involved long hours, late nights, and significant responsibility related to fiscal year-end data. The doctor stated that it might be sleep apnea, though the doctor was not sure.

Positive for nasal congestion related to fall pollen and allergies, as noted on the patient's review of systems sheet completed at check-in. Negative for nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Blood pressure in the office today is mildly elevated. The doctor noted the patient may be nervous, and that past readings are running on the higher side.

1. Congestive heart failure: Continue current medications. Increase lisinopril to 40 mg daily because blood pressure is high. Start Lasix 20 mg daily because the doctor noted the patient is retaining some fluid. Continue low-sodium diet. Repeat echocardiogram ordered. Repeat lipid panel this year.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Headache.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Donna is a 37-year-old female with a history of hypertension and diabetes who presents with headache. She reports that headaches have occurred every now and then but have recently been getting worse. She has been checking her blood pressure about once a week and reports that over the past three weeks readings have been higher than usual, including 160/87 and 175/92. Her last recorded blood pressure at a prior visit was 124/82, per the doctor. She is prescribed lisinopril and reports that she sometimes forgets to take it, particularly on weekends when she is busy. She has been checking her blood sugar, which she reports has been running around 120 and sometimes as low as 100. She reports her urination is about the same and normal. She takes Tylenol for the headaches, which provides temporary relief. Pain is rated 7/10 at onset and about 4 to 5/10 after Tylenol, with the headache still present but less pounding. The patient states she thinks the headaches could be tension headaches. She reports occasional migraines, treated rarely, but states that these headaches are different from her usual migraines. She notes it is springtime and she usually gets allergies, but states this feels very different and she has had no runny nose, cough, or congestion with the headache. She is walking regularly.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Positive for headache and intermittently elevated home blood pressure readings. Negative for nasal congestion, runny nose, and cough. Negative for increased urination. Mild tenderness reported over the forehead, cheekbones, and neck, described as mild and less than expected. Blood sugar reported as generally acceptable.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Mild tenderness to palpation of the forehead, slightly less tenderness over the cheekbones, and mild tenderness to palpation of the neck. The doctor noted no frontal or maxillary sinus tenderness and no lymphadenopathy. No other examination findings were discussed.

RESULTS
Blood pressure readings at home: 160/87 and 175/92. Prior clinic blood pressure: 124/82. Home blood glucose reported at approximately 120, sometimes near 100. No laboratory or imaging results were discussed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Headache with hypertension. The doctor notes blood pressure is significantly elevated compared with the prior visit. The patient suggested the headaches could be tension headaches. The cause of the headaches was not definitively determined in the visit. Possible contributing factors discussed include missed lisinopril doses and blood sugar fluctuations; the patient wondered if these might be causing headaches, but this was not confirmed.
   - Continue Tylenol for headache.
   - Increase lisinopril from 20 mg once daily to 40 mg once daily.
   - Continue home blood pressure monitoring.
2. Diabetes. The doctor notes blood sugar has been running somewhat high per the patient's report.
   - Order blood tests, including hemoglobin A1c and routine laboratory tests.
   - Provide diabetes education for patient review.
3. Follow-up. Return to see the doctor or Dr. Ruth after blood tests are completed to confirm stability and blood pressure control.
4. Activity. Patient asked about continuing walks; doctor advised she may continue walking and that exercise is beneficial.
